title: "Marriage means a desire and an education toward salvation, with love as its sure element" – Fr Arsenie Papacioc
attribution_note: Fr Arsenie Papacioc (1914–2011). His interview on the mystery of marriage, from Father Arsenie Speaks to Us (ed. a 2-a, vol. 1, Editura Mănăstirea Sihăstria, 2010). Translated here fresh from the Romanian with credit and a link to the source, not offered as public domain. Source: https://doxologia.ro/casatoria-inseamna-o-dorinta-o-educatie-spre-mantuire-avand-element-sigur-iubirea-pr-arsenie

sections.heading: Two paths in the world: marriage and monasticism

pairs.en: "Marriage means a desire and an education toward salvation, with love as its sure element" – Fr Arsenie Papacioc

This unity of love, of affection, of heart, which is in the family — this puts in man the power to create, with God's help. So marriage means a desire and an education toward salvation, with love as its sure element. But if you think only of pleasures, these get used up and love stops, because it withers — for the person who is not Christian.

– You say that great joy must belong to the one who gets the thought of monasticism. We want to ask you about marriage. How do you encourage young married people? Are they less close to God in the world?

– No. First of all, we too live right in the world, and we lived in the world before. Even us — the very ones who went to the monastery. But we built such a love for God, we fell into a madness for Christ, you could say. And nothing else interested us, except to glorify Him totally, with body and soul. But we're not talking now about the purpose or beauty of monasticism — we're talking about marriage.

You are in the world. Until you decide what your path of salvation is, the question is: how do you stand in the world? You marry, or you don't marry — that is, you go to the monastery. There are two positions, because there's no other way. There's a third, but it's false: "I'm not marrying, but I'm not going to the monastery either!" You live muddled and you live slobbery — that is, you're tempted from all sides, you don't even know what you want, and you have no zeal for the spiritual life. But most people marry, as God has ordained, and fewer go to the monastery.

Look, there are 5,000-6,000 monks and nuns in Romania, the most of any Orthodox country. When St. Calinic of Cernica was alive, there were 10,000. But many were closed down during those wretched 40 years of atheism.

sections.heading: The goal of marriage: mutual salvation and love

pairs.en: Let's talk about the great mass of Christians who are in the world. They face the question of marriage, of choosing the girl, of choosing the boy, with one principle: either well, or not at all. And to enter a Christian life, altogether Christian, possible for a marriage, for a house, for a family.

This marriage is not entered into for the sake of pleasure — which, mind you, is what encourages young people so much. That's a consequence. You'll have pleasures, but that's not the goal. I don't eat because the food tastes good — I eat to keep myself alive. The pleasure will come. If you're thinking about these pleasures, as many do, they'll happen. But that's not the goal.

The goal of marriage is mutual help toward salvation, stirring the other toward salvation. Because there's a hidden force, which often you can't see: you don't know what draws you toward it, toward your home or toward him. That's love, which plays a saving and creative role, always.

The fact that there's a point of attraction in marriage, that it cheers you, that you gain strength, you don't get discouraged, you're not asleep — that speaks for itself. It is the very Mystery of Marriage. Plus the children, who play a deciding role. In the end they're little angels, your mind stops when you see them moving about and when they start asking you questions. You wonder: "Who, Lord, puts these thoughts in their heads?"

So then, this unity of love, of affection, of heart, which is in the family — this puts in man the power to create, with God's help. So marriage means a desire and an education toward salvation, with love as its sure element. But if you think only of pleasures, these get used up and love stops, because it withers — for the person who is not Christian.

Marriage is an occasion for Christian strengthening of one with the other and, as I say, truly, even if it comes as a figure of speech, to fill Heaven with Christian children! Marriage deepens Heaven with Christians.

sections.heading: Monasticism: a different life and spiritual fatherhood

pairs.en: Monasticism is a different life. It's a madness for Christ, a going altogether into another world, by renouncing personality, your own will — the will God gave us. Free will, reason, and affections — all these things we have as formed points, of a whole person, like God. All these things, in monasticism you must bring them down, cut off your will, do what the other tells you even if it doesn't suit you, and take the cross and follow Me! The cross means bearing what doesn't suit you.

We give birth. Why do we call ourselves fathers? Why don't we call ourselves mothers? Our motherhood, we monks, is thousands of times greater than in the world. Because man is body and soul. And the soul is the person, not the body. And we give birth to spiritual children, being married to Christ, we being His brides. We call ourselves fathers because we give birth to ourselves. I, for instance, am the father of my own birth. I renounce everything that was in the world, free will, reason — I renounce everything. For Christ. And then I am born again. And that is why our names change at monasticism (I was called Angel and now I am Arsenie). So a monk's motherhood is far greater than one in the world. How many spiritual children do we beget, placing them on the path of salvation? How many abortions do we prevent from happening?
(Father Arsenie Speaks to Us, 2nd ed., vol. 1, Editura Mănăstirea Sihăstria, 2010, pp. 118-121)
